items.title: L8: Compound growth, real terms and recovery from a loss
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Growth questions at this level require you to think in multipliers. A quantity growing 3% a year is multiplied by 1.03 each year, so after three years it is multiplied by 1.03 × 1.03 × 1.03, about 1.093, rather than 1.09. To find an equal yearly rate over several years, take the root: a 44% rise over two years at an equal annual rate means a multiplier of 1.44, whose square root is 1.2, so 20% a year. A loss needs a larger percentage gain to recover, because the gain applies to a smaller base: after a 40% fall, a holding is worth 60% of its original, so it must be multiplied by 1/0.6, a rise of 66.7%. The rule of 72 gives a quick estimate of the doubling time: divide 72 by the annual percentage rate, so 8% doubles money in about nine years. Declining balance depreciation multiplies by a factor below one each year, for example 0.85 for a 15% fall. To find an unknown rate from a start and end value, divide the end value by the start, then take the root of the right order. Real terms adjust for inflation: a 6% pay rise when prices rise 4% is 1.06 ÷ 1.04 = 1.0192, a real rise of about 1.9%, not exactly 2%. Do not add or subtract percentages from different bases.

questions.prompt: A town of 50,000 people grows by 3% a year. What is the population after three years, to the nearest whole number?
A cost rises by 44% over two years, rising by the same percentage each year. What is the annual rate?
An investment falls by 40%. What percentage rise is needed to get back to its original value?
questions.hint: It is worth 0.6 of the original, and 1 ÷ 0.6 = 1.667.

questions.prompt: Using the rule of 72, roughly how many years does it take for a sum growing at 8% compound interest a year to double?

options.text: 18 years
8 years
12.5 years
9 years

questions.prompt: Equipment worth £40,000 loses 15% of its current value each year. What is it worth after three years, to the nearest pound?
A deposit of £8,000 grows to £9,261 in three years at a fixed rate with interest added annually. What is the annual rate?
Pay rises by 6% while prices rise by 4%. What is the approximate rise in pay in real terms?
A figure falls by 10% in each of two successive years and then rises by 20% in the third. What is the net change over the three years?

options.text: Unchanged overall
A fall of 2.8%
A rise of 2.8%
A fall of 8.8%

items.title: L8: Reading and combining two tables
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Tables in the prompt often give you rates and totals separately, and the answer needs both. Do not average percentages from groups of different size. Convert each rate to a count, add the counts, and divide by the total. If region A has 600 applications and a 30% success rate, and region B has 900 and 20%, the combined rate is (180 + 180) ÷ 1,500, which is 24%, not 25%. A mean of group means is only correct if the groups are the same size. Distinguish a share of the total from a share of a group. If 900 of 1,580 satisfied respondents used a channel, that is 57% of satisfied respondents, which is different from the channel's satisfaction rate. When a total changes, a figure can rise while its share falls: a budget line rising from £30m of £120m to £36m of £160m rose 20% but its share fell from 25% to 22.5%, a fall of 2.5 percentage points. Compare days or counts together with percentages: a fall of 6 days is twice a fall of 3 days, but if the starting points differ, the percentage falls may be close. For short forecasts, state whether the pattern is a constant amount added each period or a constant percentage. A constant amount gives a straight line, while a constant percentage compounds. Check what the question asks for before using the table.

questions.prompt: Applications and success rates: North 600 at 30%, South 900 at 20%, West 450 at 36%. What is the overall success rate across all regions, to one decimal place?
Average sick days per person: AO grade 40 staff at 6 days, EO grade 60 staff at 4 days, HEO grade 20 staff at 3 days. What is the average for all 120 staff?

options.text: 4.5 days
4.33 days
4.0 days
5.0 days

questions.prompt: Directorate X had £30m of a £120m total budget in 2023 and £36m of a £160m total in 2024. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its budget rose by 20% and its share fell by 2.5%
Its budget rose by 16.7% and its share was unchanged
Its budget rose by 6% and its share rose
Its budget rose by 20% and its share fell by 2.5 percentage points

questions.hint: Share went from 25% to 22.5%, a gap of 2.5 percentage points.

questions.prompt: A survey had 1,200 online respondents at 75% satisfied, 800 by phone at 60% satisfied and 500 by post at 40% satisfied. What percentage of all satisfied respondents used the online channel, to the nearest whole number?
A survey of 2,400 staff found 15% were under 30 and 45% were aged 30 to 49. Of those aged 50 or over, one in eight plan to retire within a year. How many is that?
questions.hint: 40% are 50 or over, which is 960, and an eighth of 960 is 120.

questions.prompt: Region P's average waiting time fell from 40 days to 34 days, and Region Q's fell from 25 days to 22 days. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both fell by about 13.5%
Q fell by more in percentage terms because it started lower
P fell by 15% and Q fell by 12%
P fell by double Q's percentage because it fell by double the days

questions.prompt: Requests in three months were 120, 135 and 150. If the percentage rise from month 2 to month 3 repeats in month 4, about how many requests are expected?
Staff in office A rose from 200 to 230, while the total across all offices rose from 500 to 560. What percentage of the total increase came from office A?
questions.hint: A added 30 of the 60 extra staff.

items.title: L8: Units, scale and compound measures
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Compound measures combine units, such as speed in miles per hour or cost per litre. Convert everything to compatible units before you calculate, and finish by checking the answer is sensible. Map scales compare a drawing with reality: at 1:50,000, 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm, or 500 m, in real life, so 3.6 cm is 1.8 km. For areas, scale factors are squared: if lengths are enlarged by 1.5, areas are multiplied by 2.25. Speed conversions use the factor 3.6: to change km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6, so 72 km/h is 20 m/s. Fuel questions combine distance, consumption and price: miles divided by miles per gallon gives gallons, and a gallon is about 4.55 litres. Time conversions need base 60: 280 minutes is 4 hours 40 minutes, not 4.4 hours. Time zone questions need you to say which direction you are moving: when a place is ahead of another, you add the difference to move there. Volume is length × width × height, and the number of boxes that fit by volume is the room volume divided by the box volume, provided all measures are in the same unit. Write units on every line of working, and cancel them as you go, so that your answer ends up in the unit that the question asks for.

questions.prompt: A map has a scale of 1:50,000. Two sites are 3.6 cm apart on the map. What is the real distance?

options.text: 3.6 km
18 km
1.8 km

questions.prompt: A room measuring 5 m by 4 m is drawn on a plan at a scale of 1:50. What is the area of the room on the drawing?

options.text: 800 cm²
40 cm²
8 cm²
80 cm²

questions.hint: The drawing is 10 cm by 8 cm.

questions.prompt: A vehicle travels at 72 km/h. What is its speed in metres per second?

options.text: 12 m/s
20 m/s

questions.prompt: A car does 45 miles per gallon. A trip of 270 miles uses petrol at £1.50 a litre, and one gallon is about 4.55 litres. What is the cost of fuel for the trip?
questions.hint: 270 ÷ 45 = 6 gallons, which is 27.3 litres, costing £40.95.

questions.prompt: A copier prints 45 pages a minute. How long does it take to print 12,600 pages?

options.text: 4 hours 20 minutes
4 hours 40 minutes
4 hours 50 minutes
4 hours 24 minutes

questions.prompt: A call is at 09:00 in New York, which is 5 hours behind London. Delhi is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of London. What time is the call in Delhi?
questions.hint: New York 09:00 is London 14:00, and Delhi is 5.5 hours ahead.

questions.prompt: A store room is 12 m long, 5 m wide and 3 m high. Archive boxes measure 0.4 m by 0.3 m by 0.25 m. How many boxes fit by volume alone?
A leaflet is enlarged on a photocopier so that each side is 150% of its original length. By what factor does its area increase?

items.title: L8: Costing decisions and option appraisal
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Costing questions ask you to choose between options. List every cost for each option, put them on the same time basis, and compare. Buying a vehicle has a purchase price, running costs and a resale value, so the annual cost is (price − resale) ÷ years, plus running costs. Leasing may be a flat annual fee. Ignoring resale value or maintenance gives a misleading comparison. Outsourcing may attract VAT that the department cannot recover, and in-house staff have on-costs on top of salary. Volume discounts usually apply only to the units above a threshold, so work out the first block and the rest separately. A payback period is the investment divided by the net saving per period, where net saving is the saving minus any running cost. Step costs jump at thresholds: if a coach seats 48 and you must move 250 people, you need 6 coaches, not 5.2. A break-even quantity is where two cost lines cross: with set-up cost S, and per-item costs a and b for two methods, break-even is S ÷ (a − b). Staff time has a cost too, found by multiplying people by hours by hourly rate. Always state which option is cheaper, by how much, and what you left out.

questions.prompt: Buying a vehicle costs £18,000, lasts 5 years, has a resale value of £3,000 and costs £400 a year to maintain. Leasing costs £3,200 a year with no other costs. Which is cheaper per year, and by how much?

options.text: Leasing, by £400 a year
Leasing, by £200 a year
Buying, by £200 a year
Leasing, by £800 a year

questions.hint: Buying costs 3,000 + 400 = £3,400 a year, compared with £3,200.

questions.prompt: In-house, a service needs 2 staff at £34,000 each, plus 30% on-costs and £6,000 of equipment. Outsourcing costs £95,000 plus 20% VAT that cannot be recovered. Which is cheaper, and by how much?

options.text: In-house, by £600
In-house, by £40,000
Outsourcing, by £19,600
In-house, by £19,600

questions.hint: In-house is 88,400 + 6,000 = £94,400, and outsourcing is £114,000.

questions.prompt: An item costs £25 each for the first 100 units and 12% less for each unit above 100. What is the cost of 340 units?
An investment of £60,000 saves £1,250 a month and costs £250 a month to run. What is the payback period?

options.text: 5 years
4 years
3.75 years
6 years

questions.hint: The net saving is £1,000 a month, so 60 months.

questions.prompt: Staff are moved by coach. Each coach seats 48 and costs £320 to hire, and 250 staff must travel. What is the total cost?
questions.hint: 250 ÷ 48 is 5.2, so 6 coaches are needed.

questions.prompt: A licence costs £450 for six months, and the team uses it 15 times a month. A pay-per-use alternative costs £6.50 a time. How much does the licence save over the six months?
questions.hint: Pay-per-use is 90 × 6.50 = £585, and the licence costs £450.

questions.prompt: Printing leaflets costs a £400 set-up charge plus 6p each. Digital printing has no set-up charge and costs 15p each. At what quantity do the two methods cost the same, rounded up to a whole leaflet?
A weekly 2-hour meeting is attended by 14 staff for 46 weeks. Staff time is valued at £28 an hour. What is the annual cost of staff time?

items.title: L8: Medians, means and spread
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Statistics questions ask which measure suits the data. The mean adds all values and divides by the count. The median is the middle value when data are in order, or the average of the two middle values if the count is even. The mode is the most frequent value. The range is the highest value minus the lowest. One very large value pulls the mean upward but leaves the median almost unchanged, so the median is often better for pay or waiting times. If you know the mean and all but one value, the missing value is the mean × count minus the known values. To change a mean when one value is replaced, find the change in the total and divide by the count. Two data sets can have the same mean and very different spread, so the range tells you about consistency. A frequency table gives how many times each value occurs: multiply each value by its frequency, add, and divide by the total frequency, not by the number of rows. A percentile rank is the share of the group scoring below a given score, so if 56 of 80 candidates scored below you, you are at the 70th percentile. When you are asked how many values lie above the mean, calculate the mean first: an extreme value can mean that only one is above it.

questions.prompt: Six values are 14, 22, 9, 31, 18 and 25. What is the median?
questions.hint: Sorted: 9, 14, 18, 22, 25, 31, so the median is (18 + 22) ÷ 2.

questions.prompt: Five salaries have a mean of £30,000. Four of them are £24,000, £25,000, £27,000 and £28,000. What is the fifth?
questions.hint: The total is 150,000 and the four known add to 104,000.

questions.prompt: Waiting times in days are 3, 5, 5, 8, 12 and 27. What are the range and the mode?

options.text: Range 27, mode 5
Range 24, mode 8
Range 27, mode 12
Range 24, mode 5

questions.hint: 27 − 3 = 24, and 5 appears twice.

questions.prompt: A candidate scores 62. In a group of 80 candidates, 56 scored lower than 62. What is the candidate's percentile rank?

options.text: 70th
77th
30th
56th

questions.prompt: The mean of 8 numbers is 25. One number, 40, is replaced by 16. What is the new mean?
questions.hint: The total falls by 24, from 200 to 176, and 176 ÷ 8 = 22.

questions.prompt: A help desk logged calls per hour over 20 hours: 0 calls in 2 hours, 1 call in 5, 2 calls in 8, 3 calls in 4 and 4 calls in 1. What is the mean number of calls per hour?
Team A's weekly sales are 20, 22, 24, 26 and 28. Team B's are 10, 15, 24, 33 and 38. Which statement is correct?

options.text: B has a mean of 24, but A's mean is lower
A has the larger range because its sales are steadier
Both have a mean of 24, so their spread is the same
Both have a mean of 24, but B's range is 28 against 8 for A

questions.hint: A's range is 8 and B's is 28.

questions.prompt: Five scores are 40, 45, 50, 55 and 110. How many of them are above the mean?

options.text: One
Three
Two
None

questions.hint: The mean is 60, so only 110 is above it.

items.title: L8: Verdicts in dense passages with several conditions
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: The hardest verdict questions pack several conditions, figures and exceptions into one short passage, and the statement tests only one combination. Work methodically. First, turn every rule into a checklist: a bursary for applicants with low household income and first-generation status needs both conditions, so the count who qualify cannot exceed the smaller group. Second, apply every condition to the case, including dates and thresholds: someone inspected 14 months ago fails a test that requires inspection within 12 months. Third, work out numbers fully before you judge: a fall of 25% from £8.0m is £6.0m, and extra spending in a different category does not change it. Fourth, notice what a statement leaves out. If a rule has an exception that depends on information not in the passage, such as advance notice of needing more time, the verdict is usually Cannot say. Fifth, compare like with like: a rise from 39% to 48% and a rise from 12% to 21% are each 9 percentage points, even though the second is a much larger relative increase. Finally, read time words carefully, such as 'next working day', since a weekend can change the answer. A statement is only True if every part is supported.

questions.prompt: "A bursary is for students from households with income below £25,000 who are the first in their family to attend university. In the first round, 120 students applied, 80 met the income test, and of those 80, 50 were the first in their family at university." Statement: "At most 50 applicants in the first round qualified for the bursary." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: 80 applicants met the income test, so up to 80 qualified
Cannot say: some applicants may be first in family but over the income limit
Cannot say: the passage does not say how many studied a priority subject
True: only those who passed the income test and were first in family qualify, and that is 50

questions.hint: Qualifying needs both tests, and 50 of the 80 income-eligible students passed the second.

questions.prompt: "An organisation may be classed as low risk if it has had no serious breach in the last three years, has been inspected within the last twelve months and has an approved risk plan. Organisation X has had no serious breach in four years, was last inspected 14 months ago and has an approved plan." Statement: "Organisation X can be classed as low risk." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not say how often low-risk bodies are inspected
True: it has gone more than three years without a serious breach
False: its last inspection was more than twelve months ago
Cannot say: it is not known whether the approved plan is up to date

questions.hint: All three conditions must be met, and one fails.

questions.prompt: "Spending on consultants fell by 25% between 2021 and 2023, when it had been £8.0m in 2021. In 2023 the department also spent £1.5m on contractors, which is not counted as consultancy." Statement: "Spending on consultants in 2023 was £6.0m." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the fall may not have been even across the two years
True: a fall of 25% from £8.0m is £6.0m
Cannot say: the 2022 figure is not given
False: with the contractors the figure was £7.5m

questions.hint: Contractor spending is excluded from consultancy.

questions.prompt: "Of 250 firms audited, 200 had at least one error in their returns. Among the firms with errors, 40% had errors in more than one area. The audit office says the sample was chosen at random." Statement: "More than 80 of the firms audited had errors in more than one area." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: 40% of the 200 firms with errors is exactly 80
True: 40% of the 250 firms is 100
Cannot say: the sample was random, so the figure may differ
Cannot say: the number of areas is not stated

questions.hint: The 40% applies to the 200 firms, not the 250.

questions.prompt: "A case is closed if the claimant does not reply within 28 days of a request for information, unless the claimant has told the service in advance that they need longer. A request was sent to Mr Ali on 1 May, and he replied on 3 June." Statement: "The service will close Mr Ali's case." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: his reply came more than 28 days after the request
Cannot say: the passage does not say when the case would be closed
False: Mr Ali did reply to the request
Cannot say: the passage does not say whether Mr Ali asked for more time in advance

questions.hint: The exception depends on a fact the passage does not give.

questions.prompt: "A national survey found that 48% of adults had used an online public service in the last year, up from 39% five years earlier. Among adults over 65, usage was 21%, up from 12%." Statement: "The rise in usage among over-65s, measured in percentage points, was smaller than the national rise." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the survey does not say how usage was measured
True: over-65s are less likely to use online services
False: both rose by 9 percentage points
Cannot say: the number of over-65s surveyed is not given

questions.prompt: "A helpline is staffed from 8am to 6pm on weekdays. Calls outside those hours go to voicemail, and the team aims to return every voicemail by noon on the next working day." Statement: "A voicemail left at 7pm on Friday will be returned by noon on Saturday." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: the team aims to return every voicemail
False: the aim is the next working day, which would be Monday
Cannot say: an aim is not a guarantee
Cannot say: the passage does not say whether Saturday is a working day

questions.hint: The helpline is staffed on weekdays only.

questions.prompt: "In 2022 a unit received 3,000 enquiries, of which 20% were about licensing. In 2023 total enquiries fell by 10%, but licensing enquiries rose to 25% of the total." Statement: "More licensing enquiries were received in 2023 than in 2022." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: 25% of 2,700 is 675, compared with 600 in 2022
Cannot say: the number of licensing enquiries is not given
False: total enquiries fell between the two years
Cannot say: the passage does not explain the rise

questions.hint: Work out both counts: 0.2 × 3,000 = 600 and 0.25 × 2,700 = 675.

items.title: L8: Parallel reasoning and matching an argument's pattern
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Parallel reasoning questions give an argument and ask which other argument has the same pattern. Ignore the topic and look at the logic. Strip each argument to a skeleton using letters. 'All A are B; C is B; therefore C is A' is invalid, because being B does not show you are A. 'All A are B; C is A; therefore C is B' is valid. Other common skeletons include: hasty generalisation, where a few cases are stretched into a rule; post hoc, where one event followed another and is said to have caused it; ad hominem, where a claim is rejected because of the person who makes it; composition, where a property of the parts is said to be a property of the whole; appeal to popularity, where something is called true because many believe it; circular reasoning, where the conclusion is simply repeated in the premise; and confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one. A valid argument and an invalid one do not share a pattern even if they look alike. Worked example: 'To enter, you need a pass; Sam has a pass; so Sam entered' has the same flaw as 'To win the contract the firm needs a bid under £2m; the bid is under £2m; so it won'. Check the form first, then the wording.

questions.prompt: "All permanent staff are entitled to join the pension scheme. Mina is entitled to join the pension scheme. Therefore Mina is permanent staff." Which argument has the same pattern of reasoning?

options.text: All qualified drivers hold a licence. Raj holds a licence. Therefore Raj is a qualified driver.
All qualified drivers hold a licence. Raj is a qualified driver. Therefore Raj holds a licence.
Some drivers hold a licence. Raj is a driver. Therefore Raj may hold a licence.
Nobody under 17 is a qualified driver. Raj is under 17. Therefore Raj is not a qualified driver.

questions.hint: Both treat 'all A are B' and 'C is B' as showing that C is A.

questions.prompt: "The last two campaigns we ran in summer failed, so any campaign we run in summer will fail." Which argument has the same pattern of reasoning?

options.text: Every audit of the unit over ten years has found errors, so the next audit will probably find errors.
Both of the last two audits of the unit found errors, so every audit of the unit will find errors.
Audits with large samples find errors, and this audit has a large sample, so it will find errors.
An audit of the unit found errors, so the unit's records must be poorly kept.

questions.hint: Both generalise firmly from a very small number of cases.

questions.prompt: "Dr Lee's report on staff retention cannot be trusted, because Dr Lee was once fined for a parking offence." Which argument has the same pattern of reasoning?

options.text: The proposal on road safety should be rejected, because the council's engineers found it unsafe.
The councillor has always supported road safety measures, so she will support this proposal.
The councillor's proposal on road safety should be rejected, because it would cost more than the budget.
The councillor's proposal on road safety should be rejected, because she once failed a driving test.

questions.hint: Both reject a claim because of a personal fact, not its content.

questions.prompt: "Complaints fell after the new director arrived, so the director must have caused the fall." Which argument has the same pattern of reasoning?

options.text: Sales rise every year before the holidays, so sales will rise before this year's holidays.
Sales rose after the poster went up, and in a similar area with no poster they did not, so the poster caused the rise.
Sales rose after the new poster went up, so the poster must have caused the rise.
The poster costs less than the sales it brought in, so it was worth displaying.

questions.hint: Both infer a cause from the fact that one event followed another.

questions.prompt: "This process is reliable because it can be relied on." Which argument has the same pattern of reasoning?

options.text: The policy is not sound because its author has no experience.
The policy is sound because it is based on sound principles.
The policy is sound because most staff say they like it.
The policy is sound because an independent review found no flaws in it.

questions.hint: Each conclusion only restates its premise in different words.

questions.prompt: "To win the contract a firm needs a bid under £2m. Firm X's bid is under £2m. So Firm X wins the contract." Which argument has the same pattern of reasoning?

options.text: To enter the building you need a pass. Sam has a pass. So Sam entered the building.
To enter the building you need a pass. Sam has no pass. So Sam did not enter the building.
To enter the building you need a pass. Sam entered the building. So Sam has a pass.
If Sam has a pass he can enter the building. Sam cannot enter. So Sam has no pass.

questions.hint: Both treat a necessary condition as if it were enough.

questions.prompt: "Every member of the team is highly efficient, so the team as a whole is highly efficient." Which argument has the same pattern of reasoning?

options.text: The team is efficient, so every member of the team is efficient.
Most of the team are efficient, so some members of the team are efficient.
Every document in the file is confidential, so the file contains confidential documents.
Every musician in the orchestra is of high quality, so the orchestra is of high quality.

questions.hint: Both assume that what holds for each part holds for the whole.

questions.prompt: "Most staff think the new system is faster, so it is faster." Which argument has the same pattern of reasoning?

options.text: Timing tests show the new bus route is shorter, so it is shorter.
The new bus route is shorter, so most residents will probably prefer it.
Most residents think the new bus route is shorter, so it is shorter.
Some residents think the new bus route is shorter, so they may use it.

questions.hint: Both treat opinion as proof of a fact that could be measured.

items.title: L8: Judging the quality of evidence
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Verbal tests often ask which evidence would best support a claim, or what is wrong with a study. Strong evidence usually has four features: a fair comparison, a large enough sample, a sound way of measuring, and reliable sources. A fair comparison uses a control group that is as similar as possible to the group being tested, ideally by random allocation. Comparing results with a previous year does not rule out other changes. A sample should be chosen so that it represents the whole group: surveying only people who finished a form leaves out those who gave up, and surveying only conference delegates leaves out the public. Small samples give unreliable results, so 6 out of 8 improving is encouraging but not conclusive. Be careful with relative figures: a '50% cut in errors' means little without the starting rate. Unusually bad results tend to improve on their own, called regression to the mean, so a before-and-after change in the worst performers is weak evidence for the treatment. Leading survey questions push respondents to a particular answer, so wording should be neutral. For sources, official statistics with a published method are usually more reliable than unnamed sources, press releases from interested groups or social media posts. Always ask what the evidence cannot show.

questions.prompt: A department wants to know whether a redesigned letter increases the number of replies. Which approach would give the best evidence?

options.text: Send the new letter only to people who have replied before
Randomly send the old or the new letter to similar claimants and compare reply rates
Send the new letter to everyone and compare replies with last year
Ask staff which letter they prefer and use the more popular one

questions.hint: Random allocation gives a fair comparison at the same time.

questions.prompt: A survey of people who completed an online form found that 92% were satisfied. What is the main weakness in using it to judge the whole service?

options.text: 92% is too high to be believable
Online surveys are always unreliable
The sample must have been too small
It leaves out people who gave up before they finished the form

questions.hint: Those who abandoned the form may be the least satisfied.

questions.prompt: Staff who did more training hours also had better performance ratings. Which further evidence would best show that training improves performance?

options.text: A survey asking staff whether they enjoyed their training
The total number of training hours across the department
Ratings for the same staff before and after training compared with a similar group who had none
A list of the most highly trained staff and their ratings

questions.hint: Before-and-after data with a comparison group addresses cause.

questions.prompt: Which source would be most reliable for the number of claims decided last year?

options.text: The department's published official statistics with a note on methods
A widely shared social media post
A press release from a campaign group
A news article quoting an unnamed official

questions.hint: Published statistics with a stated method can be checked.

questions.prompt: In a small trial, 6 of 8 patients improved. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The result is encouraging, but eight patients are too few to be reliable
The treatment works for about 75% of people
The treatment has been proved to work
The result shows nothing at all

questions.hint: Small samples can mislead.

questions.prompt: The five offices with the worst error rates were given extra training, and their error rates improved the next quarter. Which is the best alternative explanation for the improvement?

options.text: The other offices must have got worse in the same period
The offices with the worst rates had the largest teams
Unusually bad results tend to move back towards the average anyway
The training sessions were too long to be effective

questions.hint: This is regression to the mean.

questions.prompt: A press release says a new process reduces errors by 50%. What further information is needed to judge how important this is?

options.text: The names of the staff who tested the process
The number of errors before the change
Whether staff liked using the new process
How much the process cost to design

questions.hint: A 50% cut means little without the starting rate.

questions.prompt: A survey asks: "Do you agree that wasteful spending on consultants should be cut?" What is the best criticism of this question?

options.text: It does not ask about the cost of consultants
The question is too short to be useful
People will not understand the word wasteful
The wording suggests spending on consultants is wasteful, which pushes respondents to agree

questions.hint: Neutral wording is needed to get a fair view.

items.title: L8: Logic puzzles with several constraints
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Logic puzzles give several clues and ask for a placement, an order or a possibility. Work in a systematic way. Draw a simple grid or a row of boxes. Enter fixed facts first, then use each clue to eliminate options. A clue such as 'A is next to B' means that A and B occupy adjacent places in either order. A clue 'C is not next to D' removes the cases where they are adjacent. Place the most restrictive clues early, and keep checking that no clue is broken. For allocation puzzles, if a team's room is fixed by one clue, cross that room off for the others, and repeat. For truth-teller puzzles, assume a statement is true and see whether it leads to a contradiction. For overlapping groups, total = group 1 + group 2 − both when everyone is in at least one group. For calendar puzzles, count the days and use remainders: moving 19 days forward is 2 weeks and 5 days, so the weekday moves forward five places. In 'which must be true' questions, test an option by finding any arrangement that satisfies the clues and breaks the option. If you can find one, the option does not have to be true. Write your working so that you can check it again.

questions.prompt: Five colleagues, Ana, Ben, Cai, Dee and Eli, sit at desks 1 to 5 in a row. Eli is at desk 1 and Ben is at desk 3. Ana sits next to Ben. Cai does not sit next to Dee. Dee is not at an end desk. Who sits at desk 5?

options.text: Dee
Cai
Ben
Ana

questions.hint: Ana must be at 4, which leaves 2 and 5 for Cai and Dee, and Dee is not at an end.

questions.prompt: Four reports P, Q, R and S are reviewed on Monday to Thursday, one a day. P is reviewed before Q. R is reviewed the day after S. Q is reviewed on Thursday. Which statement must be true?

options.text: S is reviewed on Monday
R is reviewed on Wednesday
R is not reviewed on Monday
P is reviewed on Monday

questions.hint: R follows S, so R cannot be first.

questions.prompt: Policy, Finance and Legal each use a different room: Red, Blue or Green. Finance does not use Red. Legal uses Blue. Policy does not use Green. Which room does Finance use?

options.text: Red
It cannot be determined
Blue
Green

questions.hint: Legal has Blue, so Policy has Red, leaving Green.

questions.prompt: Kofi scored higher than Lena. Mia scored lower than Lena. Noor scored higher than Kofi but lower than Omar. Who came third?

options.text: Kofi
Lena
Omar
Noor

questions.hint: The order is Omar, Noor, Kofi, Lena, Mia.

questions.prompt: Each of two colleagues, A and B, always tells the truth or always lies. A says "B always lies." B says "We both always tell the truth." Which is the case?

options.text: Both always tell the truth
A always tells the truth and B always lies
Both always lie
A always lies and B always tells the truth

questions.hint: If B were truthful, A's statement would be false, a contradiction.

questions.prompt: In a group of 12 staff, everyone speaks Welsh or French or both. 9 speak Welsh and 7 speak French. How many speak both?
14 July is a Tuesday. What day of the week is 2 August in the same year?

options.text: Sunday
Friday
Saturday
Monday

questions.hint: It is 19 days later, which is 2 weeks and 5 days.

questions.prompt: A panel of three is chosen from Ahmed, Bea, Chen, Dana and Evan. Evan must serve, Ahmed and Bea will not serve together, and Chen serves only if Dana does. Which panel is possible?

options.text: Evan, Ahmed and Bea
Evan, Bea and Chen
Evan, Chen and Dana
Evan, Chen and Ahmed

questions.hint: Chen needs Dana, and Ahmed and Bea must not both serve.

items.title: L8: Applying rules to cases
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Many workplace verbal tests give a rule and a case and ask for the outcome. This is close to what you do when applying policy to a claim, request or application. Method: first, list each condition in the rule and whether it is joined by 'and' or 'or'. Second, check the case against each condition, using the exact facts and numbers. Third, look for exceptions and say whether the case falls into them. Fourth, decide the outcome the rule gives, not the outcome you think is fair. Pay attention to thresholds: 'over £10,000' does not include £10,000, and 'within three months' ends on the same date three months later. Where a rule gives bands, such as 70 and above, 60 to 69 and below 60, apply the band to the corrected figure, not the one first reported. Where the rule depends on a fact that is missing, such as a manager's approval, the answer is that the condition is not yet met. Worked example: a mileage allowance is paid only if public transport is unavailable. If a train was available, the allowance is not payable, even if the car was quicker. Treat each rule on its own terms, and do not mix in a different rule from memory.

questions.prompt: "A mileage allowance of 45p a mile is payable only for journeys of over 10 miles each way and only if public transport is not available. Sam drove 12 miles each way. A train was available, but it would have taken 20 minutes longer." Which outcome follows?

options.text: Payable at a reduced rate, since the train was slower
Payable, because the journey was over 10 miles each way
Not payable, because the journey was under 10 miles
Not payable, because public transport was available

questions.hint: Both conditions must be met, and the second is not.

questions.prompt: "To join the mentoring scheme an applicant must be at EO grade or below, have at least one year in post and have their line manager's agreement. Priya is an EO with 18 months in post. Her manager has not yet replied." Which outcome follows?

options.text: She cannot yet apply, because her manager's agreement is missing
She can apply, because she meets the grade and time rules
She cannot apply, because she has been in post too long
She can apply and the manager's agreement can follow

questions.hint: All three conditions are required.

questions.prompt: "Applicants scoring 70 or above are offered a place, those scoring 60 to 69 go on a reserve list, and those below 60 are rejected. A scoring error added 5 marks to every score. A candidate's reported score was 72." Which outcome follows?

options.text: The candidate is offered a place
The candidate is rejected
The candidate goes on the reserve list
The candidate is offered a place only if others decline

questions.hint: The corrected score is 67, which falls in the reserve band.

questions.prompt: "Purchases over £10,000 need three written quotes unless a framework agreement is used. A single-source purchase means buying from one supplier outside a framework or competition and needs director approval." A £14,000 purchase is made from a supplier on an approved framework. Which outcome follows?

options.text: Director approval is needed because only one supplier is involved
Three separate quotes are not needed because a framework is used
Three written quotes are needed because the purchase is over £10,000
The purchase cannot go ahead without a competition

questions.hint: The framework route is the stated exception.

questions.prompt: "Staff must tell their manager by 10am on the first day of absence. After 7 calendar days of absence, a medical statement is required." Lee was absent from Monday to the Tuesday of the following week, inclusive. Which outcome follows?

options.text: A medical statement is required, because the absence lasted 8 calendar days
A statement is not needed, because Lee missed only 7 working days
A statement is not needed until the absence has passed 10 days
A statement is needed only if Lee did not phone in on the first day

questions.hint: Monday to the next Tuesday is 8 calendar days, and the rule counts calendar days.

questions.prompt: "Gifts valued under £25 may be kept without declaring them. Gifts of £25 to £100 must be declared and may be kept only with manager approval. Gifts above £100 must be declined or handed in." A member of staff is given a gift valued at £60, and the manager has not yet approved it. Which outcome follows?

options.text: It may be kept, because it is under £100
It must be declared, and cannot be kept until the manager approves it
It must be handed in immediately
It may be kept without being declared

questions.hint: Approval is the condition for keeping a gift in this band.

questions.prompt: "Time off in lieu may be taken within three months of being earned, and unused time lapses. Ana earned 6 hours on 10 January and has taken none." Which outcome follows on 15 April?

options.text: Ana may still take the 6 hours until 30 April
Ana may take half of the hours
The 6 hours have lapsed, because three months ended on 10 April
The hours lapse only at the end of the financial year

questions.hint: Three months from 10 January ends on 10 April.

questions.prompt: "Complaints must be acknowledged within 3 working days and answered within 15 working days. If a response needs more time, the complainant must be told the new date before the 15 days end." A complaint was acknowledged on day 2, and on day 16 the complainant was told the answer would take longer. Which outcome follows?

options.text: The service broke the rule, because it did not acknowledge the complaint
The service met the rule, because the acknowledgement was within 3 days
The service met the rule, because it told the complainant eventually
The service broke the rule, because the complainant was told after day 15

questions.hint: The notice of delay had to come before the 15 days ended.

items.title: L8: Leading a team through a mistake or incident
items.body: When something goes wrong, the Civil Service Code expects honesty, integrity and accountability. A leader's first duties are to stop further harm, tell the right people quickly, establish the facts, and put things right for the people affected. After that comes learning. The Code asks civil servants to be open about mistakes and to correct them as soon as possible, and not to give false or misleading information. Good practice is a blame-free approach to learning, in which the focus is on what happened and how the process failed, while still dealing properly with any misconduct. As a leader you take responsibility for your team's work in front of others, and you support a colleague who made an honest mistake while expecting honesty from them. Practical steps are: contain the problem, for example pause further letters or payments; escalate to your manager and any specialist team, such as data protection or communications; gather facts before assigning blame; agree the corrective action and communications; record what happened; and change the process, for example by adding a check or clearer guidance. Avoid concealing errors, fixing them quietly, publicly blaming individuals, or speculating about causes before the facts are known. Worked example: your team sends wrong letters to 200 claimants. You stop further mailings, tell your manager at once, and agree how to correct and apologise.

questions.prompt: Your team has sent incorrect award letters to 200 claimants. What is the most effective first step?

options.text: Find out which team member made the error and ask them to explain
Stop further letters going out and tell your manager straight away
Wait until you know how many of the 200 have already acted on the letters
Draft corrected letters and send them before telling anyone about the error

questions.hint: Containing the problem and escalating promptly limits the harm.

questions.prompt: A junior colleague caused the error and begs you not to tell anyone. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Explain that it must be reported, offer support, and make clear it is being handled as a process failure
Tell the colleague you will report it and ask them to leave the team while it is investigated
Tell your manager it was a team error but not say who made it, to protect them
Agree to keep it between you, as it was an honest mistake and can be fixed quietly

questions.hint: Honesty about errors is required, and you can still support the person.

questions.prompt: A senior leader asks in front of the whole team who is to blame for the error. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say that nobody could have prevented the error and it should not be discussed
Name the person who sent the letters so that the leader gets a clear answer
Say you will find out who is responsible and report back to the leader on Monday
Say that you take responsibility as team leader and will work out what failed in the process

questions.hint: A leader owns the outcome, and blame can wait until the facts are known.

questions.prompt: While checking last month's work, you find the same error was made then and nobody noticed. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Check how many cases are affected and note how it happened
Report both months to your manager with the facts you have
Correct the affected cases quietly and not mention the earlier error to anyone
Ask the relevant specialist team whether anyone needs to be notified

questions.hint: Hiding a past error prevents proper correction and learning.

questions.prompt: A journalist calls the team directly asking about the wrong letters. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give the journalist the name of the manager who is leading the response
Say there is no problem with the letters while the facts are checked
Confirm there was an error and explain what happened so that the story is accurate
Say you cannot comment and pass the enquiry to the press office at once

questions.hint: The press office agrees the statement, based on confirmed facts.

questions.prompt: After the incident you are asked how to prevent a repeat. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Identify how the process allowed the error, add a check, and share what the team learned
Move the task to a more experienced person on another team
Add a second person to approve every letter, whatever the risk
Remind the team to be more careful when preparing letters in future

questions.hint: Fixing the process addresses the cause, not just the person.

questions.prompt: A team member who made a serious mistake is clearly shaken and keeps apologising. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give them quiet work for a few weeks so they can recover their confidence
Tell them it is fine and that no further discussion is needed
Reassure them, check how they are, and focus on what can be fixed and learned
Ask them to write a full account of the mistake and submit it within the hour

questions.hint: Support and learning are compatible with accountability.

questions.prompt: You realise that a figure you gave your manager yesterday was wrong, and it has been used in a briefing. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Correct the figure in the file and say nothing unless someone asks
Tell your manager immediately, give the correct figure and explain what went wrong
Tell your manager only if the briefing is about to be sent to ministers
Wait until the end of the day and then send a corrected version of the figure

questions.hint: Correct errors as soon as you find them and be open about it.

questions.prompt: The incident appears to be caused by a supplier's system, and a colleague wants to blame the supplier publicly in an email to all staff. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Send the email now, since the supplier probably caused the problem
Ask the communications team to advise on what to say and to whom
Share confirmed facts with your manager before sending anything wider
Confirm the cause with the supplier and your own technical team first

questions.hint: Blaming before the facts are known risks misleading people.

items.title: L8: Procurement integrity and supplier relationships
items.source: Civil Service Code and Government procurement guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Public procurement should be fair, open and transparent, with decisions made on the published criteria and suppliers treated equally. Civil servants must avoid conflicts of interest, protect confidential information and not give any bidder an advantage. During a competition, clarification questions from bidders are normally answered in writing and shared with all bidders, so no one has information that others lack. Contact with bidders is limited to the agreed channel, which is often the procurement team, and discussions about price or scores outside it are inappropriate. Bids and scores are confidential: sharing one bidder's details with another is a serious breach. Evaluators score against the criteria and record their reasons, so that the decision can withstand challenge. If you discover a mistake in scoring, tell the procurement lead promptly, because the correct approach may include re-scoring or informing bidders. After a contract starts, changes should follow the contract terms, and not be used to give a favoured supplier extra work without proper authority. Offers of jobs from suppliers and gifts and hospitality while a decision is open should be declared. Worked example: a bidder phones to ask whether a competitor's price is lower. You do not discuss it, and you tell the procurement lead about the call so it is recorded.

questions.prompt: During a live competition, a bidder phones you with a question about the specification. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Answer the question briefly by phone, since it is only a clarification
Ask them to send it through the agreed channel so that the answer can be shared with all bidders
Give them the name of another bidder who asked the same question
Explain you cannot talk to them until the contract has been awarded

questions.hint: All bidders must have the same information.

questions.prompt: A bidder asks you informally whether their price is the lowest. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say you cannot say, but hint that they should not worry
Say that their price is competitive, without giving figures
Suggest that they raise their price to improve their quality score
Decline to discuss prices or scores, and tell the procurement lead about the contact

questions.hint: Discussing other bids gives an unfair advantage and must be recorded.

questions.prompt: You are scoring bids and notice you have added up one bidder's scores incorrectly, which changes the ranking. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Leave it, as the scores have already been reported
Ask the bidder to confirm the corrected total before telling anyone
Tell the procurement lead straight away and follow their advice on correcting it
Correct the total quietly since the right ranking matters most

questions.hint: Errors in an evaluation need to be handled openly and under the correct procedure.

questions.prompt: A supplier whose bid you are scoring hints that they may have a job opening for someone with your skills. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell your manager and the procurement lead, and step back from the scoring
Tell the supplier politely that you cannot discuss it until the contract is decided
Score the bid as usual and raise the offer when the contract is awarded
Ignore the hint and score the bid on its merits as you normally would

questions.hint: A job offer is a conflict of interest for as long as the decision is open.

questions.prompt: A colleague on the evaluation panel shares a bidder's pricing sheet with a friend who works for another bidder. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Tell the procurement lead what you saw as soon as possible
Note down the details so you can give a factual account
Say nothing, as the damage is done and speaking up would only cause trouble
Ask the nominated officer how to raise it

questions.hint: Leaking bid information undermines fairness, and it must be reported.

questions.prompt: The contract is live and a manager wants the supplier to do extra work outside the contract, with no new competition. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the supplier to do the work and arrange payment later under another heading
Refuse any change since contracts can never be varied
Agree, as the supplier is already performing well and knows the work
Check the contract terms and ask commercial colleagues whether a variation is allowed

questions.hint: Changes must be within the contract terms and approved properly.

questions.prompt: A supplier offers your team a free training day on its products during a live tender. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Accept, as it is about learning, not entertainment
Decline, and tell your manager so it can be recorded under the gifts and hospitality rules
Accept only for the people not working on the tender
Accept if the supplier agrees to offer the same to others

questions.hint: Hospitality during a live competition risks compromising impartiality.

questions.prompt: A small local business asks you to help it write a bid, because it has not tendered before. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the procurement team to treat its bid more generously
Point it to the published guidance and the procurement team's support for all bidders
Decline to talk to it in any way during the competition
Review its draft bid and suggest changes so it scores well

questions.hint: Support must be available equally to all, with no individual coaching.

questions.prompt: A manager wants a purchase of £40,000 to go to the usual supplier without competition, "because it is quicker." Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Go ahead, as the manager has the authority and the supplier has done well so far
Check the thresholds and routes with the procurement team
Ask the manager what procurement rule allows a direct award
Suggest a compliant quick route, such as an existing framework

questions.hint: Speed is not a basis for avoiding competition.

items.title: L8: Ministers, Parliament and the press
items.source: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Management Code, GOV.UK
items.body: The Civil Service Code requires civil servants to provide information and advice, including advice to ministers, on the basis of the evidence, and accurately, honestly and truthfully. They must not deceive or knowingly mislead ministers, Parliament or the public. Ministers decide policy and are accountable to Parliament, and civil servants support them, while telling them honestly about options, risks and evidence. If a minister's decision is lawful, the civil servant implements it even if they would have chosen differently, but if it appears unlawful or improper they raise it through the proper route. Answers to Parliamentary questions must be accurate, and if an error is found, it must be corrected at the earliest opportunity through the proper channel. Official information must not be leaked, and the press office handles contact with the media. During an election period, usually called the pre-election period, departments follow guidance that limits new policy announcements and the use of resources in ways that could favour a party. Civil servants may be asked for urgent figures: they should be accurate and clearly caveated rather than guessed. Worked example: a minister's office asks for a quick statistic that you cannot yet verify. You give the verified figure, say what has not been checked, and do not guess.

questions.prompt: A minister's office needs a figure within the hour, and the only available number is a provisional estimate that has not been checked. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Round the estimate up to be on the safe side for the minister
Decline to give any number until the full data has been verified
Provide the estimate, clearly labelled as provisional, and say what remains to be checked
Provide it without labels, because a ministerial request outweighs caveats

questions.hint: Accurate information includes being clear about its limits.

questions.prompt: You are drafting an answer to a Parliamentary question and a colleague suggests wording that is technically true but would give a misleading impression. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Leave out the relevant facts so no question of misleading can arise
Use the wording, since it is technically true
Use the wording but add a footnote at the bottom
Explain that the answer must not mislead, and suggest wording that is clear and accurate

questions.hint: Answers must not mislead Parliament, even if each statement is literally true.

questions.prompt: You discover that a figure given to Parliament last week was wrong. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell your manager and the relevant team promptly so that the record can be corrected
Wait to see if anyone notices the error before taking action
Ask the minister to decide whether the error is important enough to correct
Correct the figure in the next routine publication without a statement

questions.hint: Errors in material given to Parliament must be corrected at the earliest opportunity.

questions.prompt: A minister announces a policy that you think is unwise, but it is lawful. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Raise concerns about its legality, as a way of stopping it
Tell colleagues that the policy is flawed so that they are aware
Delay your work on it until the minister has reconsidered
Make sure the minister has your honest advice on the risks, then implement it professionally

questions.hint: Civil servants advise honestly, then carry out lawful decisions.

questions.prompt: A journalist you know socially asks you informally about a decision still under consideration. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Say you cannot discuss it and refer them to the press office
Tell the journalist you will let the press office know of their interest
Give them background on the condition that they do not name you
Say that all enquiries must go through the press office

questions.hint: Briefing the press informally breaches confidentiality and the Code.

questions.prompt: You find a draft submission to a minister has been left on a train seat in a public carriage. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Throw it away so the content does not become public
Hand it in if safe, tell the department's security team and your manager at once
Leave it where it is, as the owner will probably return for it
Read through it to work out whose document it is

questions.hint: Lost official papers must be secured and reported.

questions.prompt: During the pre-election period, a manager asks you to prepare a press release announcing a new scheme. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Prepare the release and hold it until after the election
Ask a special adviser to approve it
Check the pre-election guidance and the permanent secretary's rules before doing any work
Prepare it quickly while the minister is still in office

questions.hint: New announcements are restricted in the pre-election period.

questions.prompt: An MP writes to the department about a constituent's case and asks for details of other people involved. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Share the details, as the MP represents the area and may see the data
Pass the letter to the minister's office without any other action
Refuse to reply as MPs should deal only with ministers
Reply on the constituent's case, and not disclose personal data about other people

questions.hint: Data protection rules still apply when an MP asks.

questions.prompt: You are asked to brief a minister who prefers a particular option, and you think the evidence supports a different one. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Present only the minister's preferred option, to keep the briefing short
Set out all the options with the evidence, including your honest view of which the evidence supports
Present the evidence in general terms and not recommend any option
Present the minister's option first and describe the others as unrealistic

questions.hint: Honest, objective advice is a core duty.

items.title: L8: Using digital tools and AI responsibly
items.source: Civil Service Code, UK GDPR guidance and government guidance on generative AI
items.body: Digital tools help civil servants work faster, but they bring risks that the Civil Service Code and data protection law make you responsible for. Official-sensitive and personal information should be handled only in systems your department has approved. Pasting claimant details or unpublished policy material into a public online tool, or an unapproved app, can disclose it to a third party and breach data protection and security rules. Generative AI tools can produce fluent but wrong content, including invented facts and references, so output must be checked against reliable sources before use, and you remain accountable for what you submit. Follow your department's policy on whether and how AI may be used, and be open about its use where required. Decisions about individuals, such as benefit decisions, need appropriate human oversight and must be fair and explainable. Personal devices, personal email and messaging apps should not be used for official business unless policy allows it, because records can be lost and security weakened. Do not share passwords, and report phishing or suspected compromises quickly. Worked example: you want to summarise a long internal report with a free chatbot. You check the policy, use only an approved tool, remove sensitive details if the policy allows, and check the summary against the report.

questions.prompt: You want to summarise a long internal policy paper that is not yet public, using a free public chatbot. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Check the department's policy and use only an approved tool for unpublished material
Paste in the paper but remove the title and the author's name
Paste in the paper, as the chatbot is only generating a summary
Paste in half of the paper at a time so that no one tool has it all

questions.hint: Unpublished official material belongs only in approved systems.

questions.prompt: A colleague pastes a spreadsheet of claimants' names and addresses into a public AI tool to tidy the formatting. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them to stop, and report it to the data protection or security team
Ask them to do the same for you, as it saves time
Say nothing, as the tool is only formatting the data
Tell them to delete the chat history, since this removes the data

questions.hint: Personal data was disclosed to an unapproved third party and may be a breach.

questions.prompt: An AI tool drafts a briefing for you that includes statistics and two references. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Use it as it stands, since the tool wrote it with confidence
Check every figure and reference against the original sources before using any of it
Check the references and trust the statistics
Check only the figures that look surprising

questions.hint: AI output can include invented facts, and you are accountable for what you send.

questions.prompt: A manager asks you to use an AI tool to help decide which claimants should be investigated for fraud, with no further review. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Refuse to use any digital tools for the work
Use the tool but keep its involvement confidential
Explain that decisions about individuals need human oversight, and ask what safeguards apply
Use the tool, as it will be more consistent than a person

questions.hint: Decisions affecting people must be fair, explainable and overseen by a person.

questions.prompt: You are working at home and want to forward a work document to your personal email so that you can print it. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Use the secure remote printing option, if the department offers one
Read it on screen and take notes without copying it
Ask your manager how to print securely when working remotely
Forward it, since it is only for a few minutes and you will delete it afterwards

questions.hint: Personal email is outside the department's security controls.

questions.prompt: You receive an email that appears to come from IT asking you to confirm your password by following a link. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Reply to ask the sender to prove who they are
Click the link to see whether it asks for your password
Do not click, and report it as suspected phishing using the department's route
Forward it to colleagues to warn them to ignore it

questions.hint: Phishing should be reported, and links and attachments should not be opened.

questions.prompt: A colleague uses a messaging app on their personal phone to agree a policy decision with a minister's adviser. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask for access to the chat so you can see the decision
Remind them that decisions should be recorded on official systems, and raise it with your manager if it continues
Say nothing, since many people work this way
Suggest they delete the messages to avoid trouble

questions.hint: Official business must leave a proper record on approved systems.

questions.prompt: Your department allows AI tools for drafting but asks staff to say when they have been used. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Follow the rule and note where AI has contributed, as well as checking the content
Avoid using it at all, since transparency is not required
Use it only for the parts that the reader will not notice
Use the tool freely and keep it to yourself unless asked

questions.hint: Being open about the use of tools is part of honesty and accountability.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks to borrow your login for a system because theirs has not yet been set up. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Explain that logins must not be shared and suggest chasing the access request
Offer to help with the task yourself in the meantime
Ask IT to speed up the new account
Share it for the afternoon, since you will sit with them while they use it

questions.hint: Shared logins break accountability and security rules.
